Despite their initial shock, Weeks and McCuiston kept their composure enough to draw their weapons and start shooting at von Brunn, 88. Weeks had fired his gun in the line of duty 25 years earlier as a Washington, D.C., police officer. But he said nothing compared to this bloody confrontation. "This was terrible," Weeks said softly. "This was worse. ... We lost Officer Johns." Johns died shortly after the shooting, leaving behind a family that includes a teenage son who told CNN affiliate WUSA-TV the day after the tragedy that his dad was "my hero." Watch the officers tell their story » . Just moments before their joint interview with CNN on Thursday, McCuiston and Weeks attended a grief counseling session together, and both men say they are still struggling with their emotions. The security officers said they believe von Brunn will survive his wounds and eventually face trial. Let's all remember Officer Johns, and his family, because he took the ultimate -- he did his job and he was where he was supposed to be -- and the family suffered. That could have been anyone." McCuiston and Weeks, however, deflected suggestions that they may be heroes as well because if they had not stopped von Brunn, there's no telling how many of the more than 2,000 people visiting the museum at the time could have been injured or killed. "A lot of people are going to be saying what they have been saying, 'You are a hero, you're this, you're that,' " McCuiston said. "It's like we tell everybody, 'We chose this job, it's a job. "Everyone knows when you lose someone, death is one of the worst things, even though it is reality," McCuiston said. "Time will hopefully heal all, and hopefully there will be a little bit of closure with us and the family and we can all just move forward but never forget what a wonderful man he was."

**WASHINGTON (AP)** — A security guard was shot and killed Wednesday afternoon at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum after an elderly gunman with a long history of white supremacist activity opened fire near the building's entrance, according to U.S. Park Police and museum officials.

Stephen Tyrone Johns, 39, a six-year veteran of the museum's security staff, was shot as he held open a door for visitors around 12:50 p.m. Other guards returned fire, wounding the suspect, identified by authorities as James W. von Brunn, 88, of Maryland. Johns was rushed to George Washington University Hospital, where he later died. Von Brunn was hospitalized in critical condition.

"This is a terrible day for this institution and for the country," said museum director Sara Bloomfield during a brief news conference outside the building hours after the shooting. "Steve Johns died protecting the very people who come here to learn the lessons of the Holocaust — that hatred left unchecked can kill."

## A Chaotic Scene

Witnesses described a chaotic scene as tourists and school groups fled the National Mall-area building following the sound of gunfire. The museum, which draws roughly 1.7 million visitors annually, was placed on lockdown as investigators swept the premises.

Metropolitan Police Officer Marcus Webb, one of the first responders on scene, said the speed of the museum's other guards likely prevented further casualties.

"Those officers didn't hesitate," Webb said. "They engaged the shooter within seconds. That response probably saved a lot of lives in that lobby."

A federal law enforcement official, speaking on condition of anonymity because the investigation was ongoing, said von Brunn walked through the museum's front doors carrying a rifle and began shooting almost immediately upon entry. Security personnel returned fire, striking him before he could advance further into the building.

## A Suspect With a Documented Past

Von Brunn has a decades-long history of antisemitic and white supremacist writings and activity. In 1981, he was convicted of attempting to kidnap members of the Federal Reserve Board at gunpoint, a crime for which he served more than six years in prison. He operated a website that promoted Holocaust denial and racist ideology.

The FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said they were investigating the shooting as a possible hate crime, given von Brunn's history.

President Obama, in a statement released by the White House, called the attack "a shocking and outrageous act" and offered condolences to the Johns family.

"As we saw today, this violence can be fueled by hatred of those who are different," the president said.

## Remembering Stephen Johns

Colleagues described Johns as a devoted father and a steady, well-liked presence at the museum's entrance, where he often greeted school groups and elderly visitors, including Holocaust survivors who returned regularly to share their stories.

"He had this way of making people feel safe the moment they walked in," said a fellow guard who worked alongside Johns for several years. "That was his job every single day — and he did it until the very end."

Johns is survived by his wife and young son. Family members, through a museum spokesperson, asked for privacy in the immediate aftermath of the shooting but expressed gratitude for the outpouring of support from around the country.

## Funeral Plans

Funeral arrangements were still being finalized as of Wednesday evening, but museum officials said a public memorial service was expected to be held in the coming days, with details to be announced once the family had made final decisions. # Museum Security Guards Hailed as Heroes After Deadly Shooting, But They Say They're Just Mourning a Friend

**By Staff Correspondent**

In the chaotic moments after gunfire erupted through the marble halls of the Metropolitan Arts Museum last Tuesday, it was the museum's security staff—often overlooked figures in blue blazers who spend their days answering tourists' questions and pointing toward restrooms—who became the last line of defense between a gunman and dozens of visitors.

Three guards are being credited with helping evacuate an estimated 200 patrons from the East Wing during the attack, which claimed the life of their colleague, 34-year-old Marcus Webb, a seven-year veteran of the museum's security team known to regular visitors as "the guy who always waved at kids."

But in the days since, the surviving guards have deflected almost every attempt to call them heroes.

"I didn't do anything special. I did my job," said Denise Alvarez, a 12-year employee who guided visitors through a service corridor as shots rang out two galleries away. "Marcus is the one who didn't make it home. Don't talk to me about heroes when he's not here."

## A Family, Not Just Coworkers

Those who worked alongside Webb describe a tight-knit unit that shared lunch breaks in the security office, celebrated birthdays with cake in the break room, and covered each other's shifts without complaint. Webb, they say, had a habit of learning the names of the museum's most frequent visitors and always kept hard candy in his pocket for children who grew restless during long tours.

"We weren't just people who clocked in together," said Raymond Ochoa, a guard who has worked at the museum for nine years. "Marcus used to say this job was invisible until it wasn't. None of us understood what he meant until that day."

Ochoa was stationed near the museum's rotunda when the shooting began. He described radioing colleagues, directing visitors toward emergency exits, and physically shielding an elderly couple with his own body as they moved toward safety. He grows visibly uncomfortable when asked to recount the moment in detail.

"I keep thinking about what I could have done differently. Could I have gotten to Marcus faster? Could any of us?" he said, his voice breaking. "People want to make this a story about bravery. To me, it's a story about losing my friend."

## Grief Behind the Praise

Museum officials have announced plans to name a new education wing after Webb and have set up a fund for his family, who includes a wife and two young daughters. Visitors have left flowers and handwritten notes at the museum's entrance, many addressed simply to "the guard who helped us."

Yet the surviving guards have largely stayed out of the spotlight, declining media interviews and requesting that public attention focus on Webb rather than themselves. Colleagues describe them attending grief counseling together, sitting in near silence, still processing the speed and randomness of what unfolded.

"They keep saying they don't want to be called heroes," said museum director Patricia Lin, who has worked closely with the security team for over a decade. "But I've seen the surveillance footage. I've seen what they did for people who will never know their names. Whether they accept the word or not, that's what they are."

For Alvarez, Ochoa, and their colleagues, the recognition rings hollow against the enormity of what was lost.

"Marcus should be here arguing with us about what to order for lunch," Alvarez said quietly. "Instead we're doing interviews we didn't ask for, being called something we don't feel like. We just want him back."

The museum reopened to the public this week, though the East Wing remains closed. A small memorial now sits near the entrance where Webb once greeted visitors each morning—flowers, a photograph, and a single piece of hard candy left by an anonymous visitor who remembered his kindness.
